input:
This document presents the findings of an energy assessment that has been carried out at a dairy plant, and its purpose is to build a picture of where energy is used across the site and where the most promising opportunities for improvement may lie. The assessment looks at the plant's energy position from a number of angles, taking in the current pattern of use, the refrigeration load, the steam position, and a set of recommendations that emerge from the analysis. Readers will find that the various threads are drawn together at the end of the document, where a particular measure is identified as offering the most attractive combination of saving and deliverability.

## Current use
In terms of the overall picture, electricity is the dominant energy stream at the plant, and the total electricity use amounts to some 1603 MWh per year, a figure that has been compiled from the plant's billing records over a full twelve-month period. Electricity is consumed right across the site, in production activities, in refrigeration, and in the various site services that support day-to-day operations, and it is an important feature of the profile that consumption does not simply fall away when production stops, since refrigeration and standby loads continue to draw power through idle periods. The baseline figure of 1603 MWh per year is used throughout the assessment as the reference against which potential savings are gauged, and it provides a stable foundation for the analysis. As a general observation, it can be said that measures directed at small or intermittent loads are only ever capable of recovering a limited slice of a total of this size, which is why the assessment focuses its attention primarily on the larger and more continuous loads, where the scope for meaningful savings is correspondingly greater.

## Refrigeration
Turning now to refrigeration, it is this load that accounts for the largest share of the plant's electricity consumption, and it deserves to be examined in some detail. Refrigeration at a dairy plant is essentially a continuous activity: incoming product has to be cooled down, cooled product has to be held at temperature in cold storage, and the refrigeration plant must run more or less around the clock in order to hold those temperatures steady against heat that finds its way in through the building fabric, through doorways that are opened for the movement of product and people, and from the product itself as it is brought down to its storage temperature. One consequence of this continuous character is that refrigeration looms even larger in the plant's consumption during nights, weekends and shutdown periods, when most other loads are switched off. From an energy-saving point of view, this is a significant observation, because a refrigeration plant is continuously rejecting heat at the very same time as other parts of the plant are consuming energy in order to generate heat. The opportunity that arises from this juxtaposition is explored further in the recommendations, but it is already clear at this stage that the sheer size and the unremitting continuity of the refrigeration load make it the single most important load in the plant's energy profile, and the natural starting point for any serious attempt to reduce consumption.

## Steam
The steam position is somewhat less clear-cut than the electricity position, and a degree of caution is needed in interpreting the available figures. Steam is used at the plant for a variety of heating duties, including heating product, maintaining process temperatures, and cleaning, and the figures that were available to the assessment team were drawn from one winter month. It has to be recognised that a winter month cannot be regarded as a representative sample of steam demand across the year as a whole: heating loads are inevitably at their heaviest when ambient temperatures are at their lowest and when incoming materials arrive at their coldest, so figures from such a month will tend to overstate the demand that would be seen in an average month, and it would not be sound to scale them up to an annual figure in any simple way. The assessment has therefore used the steam figures in a more limited fashion, principally to identify the main steam users and to understand the broad shape of demand through the production day. It is also worth bearing in mind that any interaction between heat recovery and duties that are currently served by steam would show itself in the steam balance rather than in the electricity figures, and the assessment has not attempted to quantify effects of that kind.

## Recommendation
Drawing the threads of the analysis together, the assessment's principal recommendation is that the plant should proceed with a heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to deliver a saving of 18% of the plant's electricity use, and in absolute terms that 18% corresponds to a saving of 289 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is estimated at $268k, which is a significant commitment, but when the saving is valued at $0.12 per kWh it is worth some $34625 per year, and on that basis the simple payback on the $268k capital cost works out at 7.7 years. It is acknowledged that a payback of 7.7 years is not a short one, and that the calculation is a simple one which does not take account of maintenance costs or of possible movements in the electricity price; it is also the case that the outcome depends on the recovered heat being used throughout the year, although the continuous nature of the refrigeration load gives good grounds for confidence on that score. The projected saving of 289 MWh per year, valued at $34625 per year, is regarded as a robust central estimate, and the recommendation is accordingly that management approve the retrofit, subject to consumption being metered after installation so that the savings actually achieved can be monitored against those projected.

## Current use
Electricity use at the plant is 1603 MWh per year, taken from billing records over a full year. Electricity is the stream the assessment can state with confidence, and it is the stream against which savings are measured. Use is spread across production, refrigeration and site services, and it does not fall to zero when production stops: refrigeration and standby loads run through idle periods, and a share of the annual total is therefore independent of output. This pattern governs what a saving measure can reach. A measure acting on a small or intermittent load can only ever recover that load's share of the total, while a measure acting on a continuous load recovers value in every week of the year. The assessment accordingly concentrates on the largest loads and on measures that act across them. The billed total is taken as recorded; it is not re-measured, and the uncertainty in the assessment sits in the projected savings rather than in the baseline they are measured against. Every figure that follows is stated against this baseline, and the recommendation at the end returns to it.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use at the plant. The load is continuous in character. Product arrives warm and is cooled; cooled product is then held at temperature in cold storage; and the refrigeration plant runs throughout to hold those temperatures against heat entering through the building fabric, through doors opened for the movement of product and people, and from the product itself while it is being brought down to temperature. Because the load never fully stops, refrigeration accounts for a larger share of annual consumption than of peak demand, and it dominates consumption during nights, weekends and shutdowns, when most other loads are off. This is the load on which the retrofit case rests. A refrigeration plant rejects heat continuously, and it rejects that heat at the same time as other parts of the plant are consuming energy to produce heat. Heat recovery takes part of the rejected heat and returns it to a duty the plant currently serves from a purchased stream. The match is structural rather than incidental: the source runs all year, and a use for recovered heat that also runs all year is what converts a rejection stream into a saving. The projected saving is stated against electricity use as a whole rather than against the refrigeration load alone, because the retrofit's effect is measured at the meter; but it is the size and continuity of the refrigeration load that make a saving of that order available at all.

## Steam
Steam serves the heating duties of the plant: heating product, holding process temperatures, and cleaning. The steam figures available to the assessment are drawn from one winter month, and they are the weakest figures in it. A winter month is not a representative sample of steam demand. Heating loads are at their heaviest when ambient temperatures are at their lowest and when incoming product and water arrive coldest, so a steam figure from that month overstates the demand of an average month and cannot be carried across the year by simple scaling. The assessment uses the steam figures only for what they can support: the identification of the principal steam users and the shape of demand across a production day. No saving is computed from them. Where heat recovery touches a duty currently served by steam, the effect falls on the steam balance; it is not counted in the electricity saving on which the recommendation is based, and it is treated here as unquantified. A steam record covering a full year would be required before the steam side of the case could be stated to the same standard as the electricity side, and obtaining that record is a measurement task, not a modelling one.

## Recommendation
Plant management is recommended to approve the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $268k. The retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, which is a saving of 289 MWh per year against current use of 1603 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is worth $34625 per year, and the simple payback on the capital cost is 7.7 years. The payback is stated before maintenance costs and before any movement in the electricity price, and it lengthens if the recovered heat displaces less electricity than projected. The condition on which the projection rests is continuity of use: the recovered heat must be taken up throughout the year, and the refrigeration load, which runs in every week, is what provides that take-up. The steam figures play no part in the saving figure, and because they come from a single winter month and are seasonal, the recommendation does not depend on them; a decision taken on the electricity figures alone is a decision taken on the sound part of the evidence. Approval should carry one condition: electricity use after installation is to be metered on the same basis as the baseline, so that the saving projected here can be checked against the saving the plant actually records.
